scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Semah originates from the mystical practices of Sufi orders and is a core ritual of the Alevi-Bektaşi belief system in Turkey.
The term derives from the Arabic 'samā‘', meaning listening, and refers to a form of devotional remembrance of God through music, poetry, and dance.
While the Mevlevi order is known for whirling dervishes, the Alevi-Bektaşi Semah has distinct forms such as the turnalar semahı and kırklar semahı.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Semah is performed during Cem ceremonies, which are spiritual gatherings central to Alevi worship, as well as at cultural festivals such as the Hacı Bektaş Veli Festival.
It serves as a ritual expression of unity with God and the natural cycles of the universe.
The dance symbolizes the soul's journey from God and its return, the cosmic order, and spiritual maturity.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Semah is danced by men and women together, often in pairs or small groups facing each other, rather than individually whirling.
Dancers perform circular movements around a central point while rotating on their own axes.
The right hand's palm faces upward, the left downward, symbolizing connection between heaven and earth.
Watch for Turnalar semahı, Kırklar semahı.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for Semah is based on the aksak rhythm, an uneven rhythmic pattern characteristic of Turkish folk and ritual music.
The primary instrument is the saz, a long-necked lute, accompanied by spiritual singing of hymns and poetry.
Listen for the Saz (long-necked lute), Tambourine, Bells, Flute.
The pulse is Aksak rhythm (uneven meter).
The music features the saz lute playing melodic lines over an aksak rhythmic base, accompanied by soft percussion and spiritual vocal chants, creating a contemplative and hypnotic atmosphere.

scenes.title: The people
narration: While no individual dancers are named in the sources, historical figures such as Hacı Bektaş Veli are central to the spiritual tradition that Semah expresses.
Rumi is associated with the broader Sufi practice of Sama but not specifically with the Alevi-Bektaşi Semah.
Within Alevi-Bektaşi communities, variants include the turnalar semahı (crane dance) and kırklar semahı (dance of the forty saints).
Semah belongs to the Sufi dhikr tradition and is closely linked to Alevi-Bektaşi religious practices centered on veneration of Ali and spiritual unity.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Semah, Alevi-Bektaşi ritual is sibling of Mevlevi Sama: Both are Sufi ritual dances involving spinning, but Mevlevi Sama is performed by men only and features individual whirling.
Semah, Alevi-Bektaşi ritual is variant of Tannoura: Egyptian adaptation of Mevlevi Sama with folk and concert dance elements.
Semah, Alevi-Bektaşi ritual is shares music of Qawwali: South Asian Sufi devotional music form related to Sama practices.
